slides.title: Material, PBR and lighting
slides.source: Source: Chapter 7, “A PBR material is a set of measurements, not a picture”; glossary, Shaders and materials.
slides.notes: A toy model: Lambert diffuse, a power-law highlight and a flat sky term. Colours are computed per pixel.
slides.picture: A sphere with one point marked and its material values listed. Then the same material under three lights. Then a light orbiting the sphere with diffuse and specular bars.

new_texts: A stack of textures and numbers that says how a surface looks.
ONE SURFACE POINT, ITS VALUES AND ITS COLOUR
Colour is 8-bit sRGB, computed from the values.
A material is not a picture. It is values per pixel: colour, metallic, roughness, normal, AO.
all_texts: A stack of textures and numbers that says how a surface looks.

new_texts: Physically based rendering: a few measured quantities per pixel, so a material holds up under any light.
THE SAME MATERIAL UNDER THREE LIGHTS
Same albedo, metallic, roughness. Three different colours.
PBR keeps those values measured, so the same material stays believable under any light.

slides.title: Albedo, roughness and metallic
slides.source: Source: Chapter 7, “A PBR material is a set of measurements”; glossary, Textures and materials; glossary, Shaders and materials.
slides.notes: Highlight widths come from the specular exponent the model derives from roughness.
slides.picture: Five swatches and five lit spheres. Then five roughness values with highlight widths. Then five metallic values.

new_texts: The colour the surface reflects, before any lighting.
SWATCH (ALBEDO) AND THE SAME ALBEDO LIT
Top: albedo as stored. Bottom: what you see.
The lit sphere is darker on one side: albedo is not the final colour.
Albedo is flat colour before any light. Lit, the same albedo shows shading.
all_texts: The colour the surface reflects, before any lighting.

Top: albedo as stored. Bottom: what you see.

new_texts: How blurred the reflections are: 0 is mirror-sharp, 1 is wide and dull.
Number under each sphere: half-width of the highlight, in degrees.
Computed from the model: highlight where the half-vector cosine^n falls to 0.5.
Rough surfaces spread the highlight: 0.10 is a 2° spot, 0.90 a 45° glow. Smoothness is 1 minus this.

new_texts: Whether the surface behaves like a metal: 0 is non-metal, 1 is metal.
Under each sphere: its diffuse part at a lit point.
A metal has no diffuse part; its colour is all reflection, tinted by albedo.
Metallic 1 removes diffuse. Metal looks dark without a bright surrounding to reflect.

slides.title: Ambient occlusion, emission and SSAO
slides.source: Source: Chapter 7, “Lighting and global illumination”; glossary, Textures and materials; glossary, Shaders and materials.
slides.notes: AO at a floor point beside a wall is 1 minus the blocked angle over pi. The SSAO bars use illustrative inputs.
slides.picture: A floor beside a wall with rays reaching a moving point. Then a dim lit surface with and without emission. Then four bars of ambient and direct light with texture AO and SSAO.

new_texts: Darkening in creases where ambient light cannot reach; direct light is not affected.
baked, in the ORM red channel
HOW MUCH SKY A FLOOR POINT SEES NEXT TO A WALL
Grey squares: AO along the floor. At the wall's foot a point sees half the sky: 0.50.
A crease sees less sky, so ambient light there is dimmer. At the wall's foot the AO value is 0.50.
all_texts: Darkening in creases where ambient light cannot reach; direct light is not affected.
baked, in the ORM red channel

new_texts: Light the surface gives off itself.
A SURFACE IN A DARK ROOM: AMBIENT 0.05, ALBEDO 0.80
output = albedo × ambient + emission. Emission needs no light to reach it.
Emission is the surface's own light. In a dark room it is the whole picture.

ambient 0.30, direct 0.70. Grey: ambient part. Black: direct, unchanged.
To judge a texture's AO, turn SSAO off, or you will not know which one you are seeing.

slides.title: ORM, channel packing and slot naming
slides.source: Source: Chapter 7, “StandardMaterial3D, ORMMaterial3D, ShaderMaterial”; glossary, Textures and materials.
slides.notes: Texel values are generated from a seeded random source.
slides.picture: Three small grey maps combine into one coloured map. Then one texel is split into its three channel values. Then three file names go to three material slots.

new_texts: A packed map: occlusion in red, roughness in green, metallic in blue.
THREE GREY MAPS BECOME ONE COLOURED MAP
One file, three maps. Fewer files to load, and the GPU reads all three with one lookup.
all_texts: A packed map: occlusion in red, roughness in green, metallic in blue.
THREE GREY MAPS BECOME ONE COLOURED MAP
One file, three maps. Fewer files to load, and the GPU reads all three with one lookup.

new_texts: Storing different maps in the red, green and blue channels of one image.
As a picture it is just a colour. Read per channel, it is three maps.
Packing is just assigning a map to each channel. The reader must know which channel is which.

slides.title: Smoothness, HDRP mask map and URP maps

new_texts: The inverse of roughness: how mirror-like a surface is.
Smoothness is just 1 minus roughness. The numbers run the opposite way.

slides.title: UV, unwrapping and baking
slides.source: Source: Chapter 6, UV; glossary, 3D assets and Blender; Riot Ep 3, Character Art; glossary, Shaders and materials.
slides.notes: Point positions are interpolated from the triangle’s vertex UVs; the cube cut count is faces, edges and folds.
slides.picture: A triangle on a mesh and the same triangle in a 4 by 4 checker texture with a moving point. Then a cube cut into a flat net. Then a bumpy profile baked into a normal map on a flat low-poly surface.

new_texts: 2D coordinates that map each point of a surface to a spot on a texture.
A POINT ON THE MESH LANDS ON A TEXEL
texel column 2, row 2 from the top
Each mesh point stores a (u, v). The engine reads the texel at that spot, so the checker follows the surface.
all_texts: 2D coordinates that map each point of a surface to a spot on a texture.
A POINT ON THE MESH LANDS ON A TEXEL

new_texts: Cutting a mesh along seams and flattening it into a UV map.
A CUBE CUT OPEN: 6 FACES, 12 EDGES
faces 6, edges 12, a net keeps 5 as folds
so 7 edges are cut: those are the seams (red).
Cut fewer edges and the texture stretches; cut more and it splits.
Unwrapping cuts along seams and lays the surface flat. A cube needs 7 cuts.

slides.title: Resolution, texel density and UV scale
slides.source: Source: Chapter 2 and 7 (texture sizes); glossary, Textures and materials.
slides.notes: Density = texture pixels × UV scale ÷ metres.
slides.picture: A circle drawn at 8, 16 and 32 pixels across. Then a 2 metre wall and an 8 metre wall with the same 1024 pixel texture and their densities. Then the 8 metre wall with UV scale 4.

new_texts: Width and height of a texture in pixels.
THE SAME CIRCLE AT THREE RESOLUTIONS
Four times the pixels for every doubling of width.
Resolution says how big the image is. A 1024 × 1024 map holds a million texels.
all_texts: Width and height of a texture in pixels.

Four times the pixels for every doubling of width.

new_texts: Texels per unit of world size: texture pixels per metre. Should match across objects.
512 versus 128: the checker squares are four times coarser on the long wall.
density = texture pixels × UV scale ÷ metres of surface
Density says how sharp it looks on the surface. Same image, longer wall, blurrier look.

UV SCALE 4 ON THE LONG WALL

slides.title: Tiling, wrap mode and mipmaps
slides.source: Source: Chapter 7, import options; Chapter 2, mipmaps; glossary, Textures and materials.
slides.notes: Mip chain 1024 to 1 is 11 levels; the sum of quarter-size levels is 1.333 of level 0.
slides.picture: A ramp texture that jumps at every join and a periodic texture that does not. Then repeat and clamp read past the edge. Then a chain of mip levels and the extra memory.

new_texts: Repeating a texture across a surface; a seamless texture shows no join.
Dashed lines: where tiles meet. A jump there is a visible seam.
Tiling repeats one texture over a long surface. A seamless texture has no jump at the join.
all_texts: Repeating a texture across a surface; a seamless texture shows no join.

new_texts: What sampling outside 0 to 1 does: repeat (tile) or clamp (stretch the edge).
SAMPLING PAST THE EDGE: u FROM 0 TO 1.6
Repeat wraps back to 0. Clamp holds the edge pixel, which streaks when stretched.

slides.notes: Shadow test is computed per floor cell. The bounce factor 0.40 is illustrative.

SUN LOW ON THE LEFT; THE BOX MOVES
baked: made once at bake time
The baked shadow stays where the box was. It cannot follow a moving object.
Bake once, play many times. Cheap and soft, but a baked shadow cannot move with the object.

new_texts: Is each map colour or data, and decoded that way?
Is the normal map tangent space, green up for Godot?
Which channel does each packed map read: R, G, B?
Is texel density the same on neighbouring objects?
Are mipmaps on, and is wrap repeat or clamp as intended?
Under which lighting did I judge it?
Then say it exactly: not “make it metal”, but “metallic 1.0, roughness 0.3”.
